title: Terminal and Horizon
premise: Jude Sterling, navigator of the salvage freighter Vesper, has spent years keeping the derelict beacon at Terminal Station running—a monument to a commissioning order no one will claim. When a distress call arrives in a language extinct since the Diaspora Wars, Jude decodes it and learns the beacon was built to mask a prison ship full of illegal consciousness backups: people the fleet erased rather than rescue. As the fleet's fragile truce nears expiry and a warship closes in to silence the signal forever, Jude must choose between loyalty to the crew who sheltered them and truth for the sleepers in the hold. Racing to the Horizon relay at the edge of dead space, Jude broadcasts the backups' testimony, forcing the fleet to acknowledge its crime—and chooses to stay with the freed minds rather than return to a world that never wanted them.
about_author: Rafael Kavanagh is a former maritime radio operator who spent a decade relaying signals along remote shipping lanes before turning to fiction. Their work explores what survives when institutions decide a person no longer counts.

chapters.title: The Beacon Nobody Ordered
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Aboard Terminal Station, Jude performs the daily maintenance ritual on the ancient beacon, cataloguing its impossible provenance while the freighter Vesper docks for supplies. Crew banter reveals Jude's isolation—respected, never included. Emotional beat: quiet loneliness disguised as competence.

chapters.title: Backups Sleeping in the Hold
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The Vesper takes on sealed cargo crates that hum at night; engineer Sefa warns Jude never to open them. Jude dreams of voices counting in an old dialect. Emotional beat: unease—the first crack in the comfortable invisibility Jude has built.

chapters.title: A Language Extinct for Two Centuries
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The beacon intercepts a distress signal in pre-Diaspora Kessari, a language Jude only knows from their grandmother's lullabies. They translate fragments: 'we are not cargo.' Emotional beat: shock and recognition, as the past speaks directly to them.

chapters.title: Commissioning Order 77-K
chapters.summary: Jude's POV, with flashbacks. Digging through station archives, Jude finds the beacon's original order—signed by a fleet admiral, ordering a signal mask over coordinates where something was buried. The order was never rescinded. Emotional beat: dread hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: Sefa's Silence
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. The engineer confronts Jude privately, revealing she knows what's in the hold: consciousness backups salvaged from the prison ship Erebus, kept dormant because waking them is a capital crime under fleet law. She asks Jude to let it go. Emotional beat: loyalty offered as a cage.

chapters.title: The Truce Clock
chapters.summary: Captain Idris's POV. Fleet broadcast announces the border truce expires in nineteen days; after that, salvage rights—and inconvenient evidence—belong to whoever claims them first. Idris orders course toward the Horizon relay, telling no one why. Emotional beat: cold pragmatism masking fear.

chapters.title: Waking One
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Against orders, Jude opens one crate and interfaces with a backup: a Kessari archivist named Oyelaran who remembers her own erasure. She confirms the beacon masks a massacre. Emotional beat: grief and awe—contact with a ghost who is alive.

chapters.title: What the Crew Deserves to Know
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Jude tells the crew the truth; the Vesper fractures. Navigator's mate Dov wants to sell the backups to the highest bidder; medic Anouk sides with Jude. Emotional beat: betrayal and solidarity colliding in a cramped galley.

chapters.title: Signal Ghosts
chapters.summary: Oyelaran's POV (rendered through the interface). She walks Jude through the Erebus's final hours—two thousand minds told they were being archived for safety. Emotional beat: intimate horror, and the birth of a vow between them.

chapters.title: The Warship Meridian
chapters.summary: Fleet Captain Vashti Roque's POV. The warship Meridian detects the beacon anomaly and alters course. Roque, a career officer with her own erased family records, begins to suspect what Order 77-K concealed. Emotional beat: duty straining against dawning shame.

chapters.title: Nineteen Days, Then Nine
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. The Vesper burns hard for dead space, but the hold's life-support draw forces rationing; waking more backups means starving the crew's margins. Dov attempts to jettison two crates. Emotional beat: moral triage—every choice costs someone.

chapters.title: Mutiny at the Airlock
chapters.summary: Anouk's POV. Dov's sabotage fails; in the struggle, a crate cracks and a second backup wakes screaming. Idris, forced to choose, confines Dov and commits the ship to Jude's plan—but privately warns Jude he expects payment at Horizon. Emotional beat: relief shadowed by debt.

chapters.title: Dead Space Navigation
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Navigating unmapped space, Jude uses the beacon's hidden frequency as a guide—discovering Order 77-K left a breadcrumb trail meant for someone who would eventually come looking. Emotional beat: wonder; the invisible work of years becomes a lifeline.

chapters.title: Roque's Dilemma
chapters.summary: Roque's POV. The Meridian overtakes a fleeing smuggler carrying Erebus records; reading them, Roque finds her grandmother's name among the erased. She delays her report by six hours—an act of treason measured in paperwork. Emotional beat: grief weaponized into quiet defiance.

chapters.title: The Hold Wakes
chapters.summary: Oyelaran and Jude's shared POV. With time short, they wake forty backups to help decode the relay protocols. The hold becomes a crowded, singing city of the displaced. Emotional beat: belonging—for the first time, Jude is among people like them.

chapters.title: Horizon Relay
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. The Vesper reaches the relay, a rusting cathedral of antennas at the edge of charted space. Idris demands his payment: the beacon's commissioning codes, worth a fortune in salvage law. Jude realizes he planned this all along. Emotional beat: the price of loyalty made explicit.

chapters.title: Meridian Arrives
chapters.summary: Roque's POV. The warship drops out of burn at Horizon, weapons hot, truce hours from expiring. Roque hails the Vesper—not with an arrest order, but a question: 'Who gave you that frequency?' Emotional beat: standoff as conversation, enemies circling a shared wound.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Climax. As the truce expires, Jude uplinks the backups' testimony through the relay on all fleet bands—names, dates, the text of Order 77-K. Roque refuses the order to fire, citing chain-of-command illegitimacy. Emotional beat: truth as an act of war and mercy at once.

chapters.title: Aftermath of a Signal
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The broadcast spreads faster than the fleet can suppress it; colonies with erased ancestors begin demanding records. Idris sells his codes anyway and vanishes; Dov, released, chooses to stay and help. Emotional beat: messy, incomplete justice taking root.

chapters.title: Tribunal at Terminal
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Months later, a civilian tribunal convenes aboard Terminal Station. Jude testifies, refusing amnesty that would require silence about the crew's crimes. Oyelaran speaks for the restored. Emotional beat: accountability chosen over escape.

chapters.title: The Beacon Remembered
chapters.summary: Oyelaran's POV. The beacon is decommissioned as a mask and recommissioned as a memorial transmitter, broadcasting the names of the erased on a loop. Oyelaran tends it now, teaching its language to children born after. Emotional beat: mourning transformed into inheritance.

chapters.title: Terminal and Horizon
chapters.summary: Jude's POV. Epilogue. Offered a fleet commission and a pardon, Jude declines, staying at the renamed station between the terminal of one life and the horizon of another. The final signal sent is a Kessari lullaby. Emotional beat: peace earned, belonging chosen at last.
